title: How does Kafka handle backpressure, and how does it affect consumer lag and throughput (pull model, manual offset, scaling consumers)?
shortTitle: How Kafka handles backpressure and its effect on lag and throughput
keyPoints: Kafka uses a pull model: consumers call poll() to fetch records at their own pace, so a slow consumer simply polls less.
Unprocessed records remain in the durable log (bounded by retention), so nothing is lost under backpressure.
The visible effect of backpressure is consumer lag: the backlog in the log that the consumer has not yet processed.
max.poll.records bounds each poll batch; if a batch overruns max.poll.interval.ms the broker triggers a rebalance.
Manual offset commit (auto.commit=false) keeps lag honest because committed position reflects real completed work.
Throughput scales by adding consumers up to the partition count; beyond that, add partitions.
Kafka converts overload into durable lag instead of failure, which buys time to react.

s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka's pull model gives backpressure for free, so a slow consumer fetches less and the backlog becomes durable lag rather than overload, and you raise throughput by tuning fetch sizes and scaling consumers up to the partition count.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Pull model** -- consumers call `poll()` to request records at their own pace; the broker never pushes records onto a consumer.
- **Durable lag** -- unprocessed records remain safely in the partition log, bounded only by retention, so backpressure means a growing backlog, not lost data.
- **max.poll.records** -- caps how many records one poll returns, bounding the batch the consumer must process before the next poll.
- **max.poll.interval.ms** -- the deadline by which the consumer must call poll again; exceeding it triggers a rebalance.
- **Manual offset commit** -- committing only after processing keeps the committed position truthful, so lag honestly reflects outstanding work.
- **Scaling consumers** -- adding consumers up to the partition count raises throughput; beyond that, add partitions.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's documents arriving in a big filing cabinet (the Kafka log). A push system would be a conveyor belt dumping documents onto a clerk's desk faster than the clerk can file them, burying the clerk. Kafka's pull model is different: the clerk walks to the cabinet and takes only as many documents as they can handle. If the clerk is slow, they take fewer and the cabinet holds the rest safely. The growing pile in the cabinet is the lag. To go faster, you hire more clerks, up to the number of drawers.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka handles backpressure almost for free because it is pull-based. Consumers call poll() to fetch records at their own pace, so a busy consumer simply polls less and fetches smaller batches. Unprocessed records remain safely in the durable partition log, and the growing backlog shows up as consumer lag rather than lost data or memory pressure.

Managing backpressure means tuning poll size to stay under the poll interval deadline, committing offsets manually so lag is honest, and scaling consumers up to the partition count. Beyond that, add partitions. The pull model is why Kafka stays stable under bursty load while push-based queues can overwhelm a slow consumer.

At National Bank of India, the settlement consumer calls a slow risk engine, so during market hours it falls behind and lag grows. Rajesh reduced max.poll.records to keep each batch within the poll interval, switched to manual commit, and scaled the consumer group to match the partition count. The lag drains after market hours.

Remember one sentence: Kafka turns overload into durable lag instead of failure, which buys you time to react, and throughput scales by adding consumers up to the partition count.
